fulldatas.lawyer:
M Golam Rabbani with AKM Asaduzzaman, Advocates ----- For the Appellants.  
AY Salehuzzaman, DAG  ----- For the Respondents.
fulldatas.parties:
Noor Mohammad Khan & ors ----- Appellants  
Vs. 
Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh & ors ----- Respondents
fulldatas.full_judgment:
Kazi Ebadul Haque J: This appeal is at the instance of the plaintiff against the judgment dated 28th August, 1982 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 401 of 1979. 

 2. The case of the plaintiffs, inter alia, was that the suit plot No. 5 measuring an area of 45.93 acres of land belonged to Dhaka Nowab Court of Wards Estate as the recorded owner in the CS Khatian No. 1 of mouza Chowbaria under Police Station Savar, District Dhaka and the said Court of Wards Estate settled the said land in rayoti right to the plaintiff No. 1 on 20.6.1353 BS by granting Amalnama and rent receipt in his favour on receiving salami; that the plaintiff No. 1 settled part of the suit land to some tenants and he remained in possession of 28.79 acres of land after such settlement; that the plaintiff No. 1 subsequently gifted another portion of the suit land to his children, plaintiff Nos. 2-5 and thus all the plaintiffs remained in possession of the suit land; that at the initial stage of the SA settlement operation the suit land was recorded in the name of the plaintiff No. 1 but the defendant No. 2 most illegally and behind the back of the plaintiff No. 1 got the suit property recorded in SA khatian in the name of the defendant No. 2; that subsequently in RS khatian the same mistake was committed by recording the land in the name of the defendant No. 2; that the plaintiff No. 1 who was away from the country could not know about the wrong recording of the name of defendant No. 2 in the SA as well as RS Khatian; that the wrong recording of the suit land in the RS Khatian cast cloud over the title of the plaintiffs in the suit land giving rise to the cause of action of the suit. 

 3. Defendant Government of Bangladesh contested the suit by filing a written statement denying material allegations and stating, inter alia, that the suit is barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and is not maintainable; that the defendant government further denied that the Dhaka Court of Wards Estate settled the suit plot to the plaintiff No. by granting amalnama or rent receipt on receipt of salami or that the plaintiff No. 1 leased out some portions of the suit plot to some tenants and the suit land remained in his possession or that the plaintiff No. 1 gifted some portion of the suit property to plaintiff Nos. 2-5 or that the plaintiffs have been owning and possessing the same peacefully. The further case of the defendant Government is that the suit plot was declared as reserved forest under Gazette Notification No. 3125 dated 13.4.55 published in the Dhaka Gazette on 5th May, 1965 and subsequently the Nowab Estate was acquired by the Government under the provision of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Since the aforesaid Gazette Notification suit plot is in peaceful possession of the Forest Department. The Exlandlord of Dhaka Nawab Estate entered into an agreement with the Collector of Mymensingh and Dhaka on 26.1.1923 for the management of the forest and as such ex-landlord had no right to settle the suit plot to the plaintiff No. 1. The suit plot having been correctly recorded in the name of the Forest Department in the SA and RS Khatian, the suit is barred under section 144B of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The plaintiffs in order to grab the forest land of the Government have filed the suit on the basis of forged, fabricated, ante-dated and fraudulent papers. The plaintiffs did not acquire any right, title, interest or possession in the suit land on the basis of the alleged amalnama and rent receipt. 

 7. Mr. M Golam Rabbani, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff appellants, submitted that the court below was wholly wrong to hold that the basic documents of the plaintiff could not be satisfactorily proved and that plaintiffs also failed to prove their physical possession in the suit land inasmuch as the plaintiff No. 1 as PW 1 proved the document marked Ext. 1, receipt showing payment of salami, Ext. 2, the Amalnama and Ext. 3 series, rent receipts granted to him by the Dhaka Nowab Court of Wards Estate for the years 1353, 1354 and 1358 B.S. He further submitted that the court below was wholly wrong to find that PW 5 utterly failed to prove the documents as he does not know how to read and write when PW 5 simply corroborated the statement of PW 1 as regards settlement of the suit land to the plaintiff No. 1. He further submitted that the plaintiffs did not attempt to prove the document through PW 5. He further submitted referring to section 47 of the Evidence Act that documents could be proved by a witness who knows the hand-writing of the person writing the document and signature of the person who signed the same. He also referred to a decision reported in the case of Ram Chandra and another Vs. Jaithmal and others reported in AIR 1934 All at page 990 wherein it was held that a person who cannot read and write certain characters may prove the hand-writing of another in those characters. The learned Advocate next submitted that the plaintiffs having discharged the onus lying on them by proving the documents in support of their title in the suit land onus shifted on the defendants to rebut the same by producing the counter-foils of rent receipts lying in their custody and the defendants though challenged the genuineness of plaintiffs documents failed to produce any oral as well as documentary evidence to disprove the same. The learned Advocate also referred to Order 18 rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure in support of his contention. The learned Advocate next submitted that the court below was wholly wrong in holding that the plaintiffs failed to prove possession in the suit land inasmuch as the plaintiffs must be presumed to be in possession as they proved their title thereof specially when defendants failed to prove their possession by adducing any evidence inasmuch as the plaintiffs adduced some evidence in support of their possession in the suit land. The learned Advocate for the appellant further submitted that the notification under section 4 of the Forest Act could not vest the suit property with the Government or the Forest Department. 

 8. Mr. AY Salehuzzaman, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the defendant Government, submitted that in paragraph Nos. 5-7 of the plaint the plaintiff asserted that SA Khatian as well as RS Khatian in respect of the suit land was wrongly recorded in the name of the defendant Government. Under section 144A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, there is presumption of correctness of the entry made in the RS Khatian and as such presumption of possession of the suit land is in favour of the defendant Government and the plaintiffs having failed to satisfactorily prove their possession in the suit land, the suit for mere declaration of title without prayer for consequential relief by way of either confirmation or recovery of possession of the suit land is barred under the provision of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The learned Deputy Attorney-General further submitted that the plaintiffs asserted in the plaint that at the initial stage of preparation of record of rights the name of plaintiff No. 1 was re-corded in the S.A. khatian and subsequently the same was wrongly recorded in the name of the defendant No. 2 and R.S. khatian is simply a copy of the S.A. khatian and that part of the suit plot was leased out by the plaintiff No.1 to some of the tenants and the same were recorded in their names but the plaintiffs failed to produce any khatian to show that part of the suit plot was recorded in the name of the alleged tenants of plaintiff No. 1 or compensation assessment roll for payment of compensation to the plaintiff No. 1 for the said tenanted land was prepared in the name of the plaintiff No. 1. Moreover, the plaintiffs could not produce any rent receipt granted either to them or to their tenants after the acquisition of Dhaka Court of Wards Estate by the Government. He further submitted that as the plaintiffs failed to prove their case there was no question of discharging onus by the defendant Government by adducing oral evidence or by producing counter-foils of rent receipts genuineness of which was challenged by the defendant Government. 

 10. We are to consider here whether the plaintiffs have been able to prove their title to the suit land. Ext. 1 is the receipt for payment of salami to the Dhaka Nowab Court of Wards Estate. Ext. 2 is the alleged Amalnama granted by the said Estate settling the suit land to the plaintiff No. 1 and Ext 3 series are the rent receipts granted for the years 1353, 1354 and 1358 B.S. by the said Estate. The appellants have not included the said documents in the Paper Book though the Rules provide that part II of the Paper Book shall consist of exhibits and no finding or conclusion in the decision appealed from will be permitted to be challenged at the hearing of the appeal unless the materials on which such challenge is based is included in the Paper Book. As such we are not bound to consider the said documents. However, we have perused the said documents in the lower court records. The contents of Exts. 1 and 3 series were written with pencil and Ext. 2 with ink as pointed out by the learned Deputy Attorney-General. He also pointed out that the receipts were rubbed to make the same appear old and the same were written with pencil instead of ink so as to avoid the same from being checked. We have noticed from Ext. 1 that the amount of salami was received subject to the approval of the Chief Manager and from the remarks in the bottom of the said Ext No. 1 it appears that salami and rents received without approval of the Chief Manager will not have the effect of settling the land of the Estate to the person paying the same. We find from Ext. 2 that it is a form of proposal for settlement of the land of the said Estate and there was no approval of the Chief Manager. We have also noticed from Ext. 3 series, rent receipts that unless settlement is approved by the authorised officer of the Estate claim or settlement of land cannot be made on the basis of payment of rent. In Ext. 2 it has also been clearly written that the proposal for settlement of land will not be effective unless the tenant executes kabuliyat in favour of the landlord. The plaintiff No. 1 as PW 1 stated that the receipt for payment of salami was signed by Gobinda Chandra Roy, Cashier of Dhaka Nowab Estate in his presence and the said receipt was marked Ext. 1. The said witness further stated in his deposition that the suit land was leased out to him by the document of lease executed by the officers of Nowab Estate including Assistant Manager, Dhaka Nowab Estate by signing before him and the document was marked Ext. 2. He further stated that these are the signatures of the Head Assistant and Assistant Manager in the said document marked Exts. 2(i) and 2(ii). He further stated that he paid rent to the Nowab Estate afterwards and rent receipts were granted by the Dhaka Nowab Estate and the same were marked Ext. 3 series. From the cross-examination of this witness we find that he was a school student at the relevant time of taking lease and that he did not pay any rent from 1359 BS upto date. PW 5, who claimed himself to be an ex-employee of Dhaka Nowab Court of Wards Estate as orderly of the then Assistant Manager, stated in his deposition that the Assistant Manager Abul Kashem executed Ext. 2 in his presence and proved his signature marked Ext. 2(ii). He further stated that receipt of salami Ext.1 and rent receipts were granted by Dhaka Nowab Estate. From his cross-examination, we find that he is an illiterate person and he could not satisfy the court that he ever worked as orderly of the said Estate. We are unable to place any reliance on the testimony of PW 5. He appears to be a procured witness who does not know how to sign his name and put his thumb impression in the deposition sheet. PW1 being the plaintiff and a school student at the relevant time on his own admission cannot also be relied on as he is interested in the result of the suit. The contents of the said documents were not even attempted to be proved by the PW1. Considering the evidence of the said witnesses we arc of the view that the said documents were not legally proved as writing of the said documents could not be proved by examining any witness. We are unable to appreciate the argument of the learned Advocate of the appellants that the said documents were legally proved. The decision referred to by the learned Advocate has no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the instant case. From the very look the said documents appear to be spurious and manufactured for the purpose of the suit in collusion with the interested persons. Even if these documents are accepted as genuine the same could not create title in favour of the plaintiffs in the absence of the approval by the Chief Manager and execution of kabuliyat in compliance thereof. It appears that the alleged settlement by the said document were not acted upon as the plaintiffs failed to produce any rent receipts granted by the Government after the acquisition of rent receiving interest nor they could produce any khatian alleged to be prepared in the name of their alleged tenants in respect of part of the suit plot or any compensation assessment roll in the name of the plaintiffs or in respect of the said tenanted land or any khatian alleged to have been prepared in the name of the plaintiff No. 1 at the initial stage. Moreover, the PW 1 himself admitted that he did not pay rent from 1359 BS upto date. 

 13. Though the Government did not examine any witness they produced copy of Dhaka Gazette dated May 5, 1955 publishing Notification No. 3125-For-13th April, 1955 under section 4 of the Forest Act, 1927 in respect of the suit plot No. 5 of Mouza Chowbaria. This Notification is a preliminary of vesting of the land contained in the said notification. The Government did not take any step to produce the Notification under section 20 of the Forest Act which is a natural culmination of a preliminary Notification under section 4 of the Forest Act. As we have already found that the plaintiffs failed to prove their title or possession in the suit land there is no necessity of deciding whether the suit land vested in the Government as reserved forest land. Admittedly SA khatian and subsequently prepared and published RS khatian are in the name of the defendant No. 2 Forest Department. RS khatian prepared under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act has presumption of correctness under section 144A of the said Act. The plaintiffs having failed to displace the said presumption by proving their title and possession in the suit land the plaintiffs are not entitled to any decree and the learned Subordinate Judge rightly dismissed the suit.

fulldatas.parties:
Jahangir Nagar University Co-operative Housing Society ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Mujibur Rahman (Md) & others ----- Opposite Parties
fulldatas.full_judgment:
This Rule was earlier issued under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure against an order dated 15-11-1989 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Savar, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 372 of 1984. The learned Assistant Judge by the said order allowed the amendment of the plaint in respect of schedule attached to the plaint. 

 2. The petitioner's case in short is that the plaintiff-opposite-parties instituted Title Suit No. 288 of 1976 in the 2nd Court of Munsif, Dhaka which was subsequently transferred to the Assistant judge, Savar, Dhaka and re-numbered as Title Suit No. 372 of 1984 for a declaration of title in the suit properties wherein the defendant petitioner was added subsequently. The further case of the petitioner is that the plaintiff instituted the suit alleging that 4.48 acres of land of plot No. 148 of Touzi No. 8173 of mouza Salia under Police Station Savar, District Dhaka originally belonged to the Dhaka Nowab Estate out of which 3.79 acres of land was given in settlement by the Manager of the said Estate under his memo. No. 591 DG 15-8-51 to one Abdur Rashid Bepari son of Abdul Jabbar Fakir of Miton and on receipt of Salami granted receipt on 6-3-58. Said Abdur Rashid Bepari possessed and enjoyed the said land and paid rent to the Nowab Estate upto 1361 BS and during the settlement operation the land was recorded in the name of said Abdur Rashid Bepari at PRR stage. But it was omitted in the copy prepared under section 46 of Estate Acquisition and Tenancy Act and as such objection raised in case No. 73 of 1964 and subsequently the land was recorded in the name of Abdur Rashid Bepari by opening khatian No. 38 who duly paid rent and got DCR. It is also the case, of the plaintiff that the name of said Abdur Rashid Bepari was recorded in the present RS khatian. Thereafter Abdur Rashid Bepari sold the suit properties to different persons including plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2. Plaintiff No. 2 transferred 76 decimals of land to the plaintiff No. 3 out of his purchased 95 decimals and plaintiff No. 4 purchased 1.89 decimals of land from other transferee of Abdur Rashid Bepari. Thereafter when the plaintiffs applied for mutation of their names in the RS khatian they found the name of Saidur Rahman already mutated in the khatian. The plaintiffs then filed Misc. Case No. 34 of 1975 before the defendant No. 1 who found that the Circle Officer (Rev) was not the competent authority to record the name of predecessor of Abdur Rashid Bepari and mutation of Saidur Rahman's name was also found illegal and order passed for cancellation of the name of Abdur Rashid Bepari and treated the suit properties as government khas land and that compelled the plaintiffs to file the present suit for declaration that the orders of the defendant No. 1 dated 6-8-1987 are illegal, null and void and the plaintiffs are the lawful owners of the suit property. 

 3. Defendant-opposite party No. 5 and the present defendant-petitioner contested the suit by filing written statement. It is the case of the present petitioner that the land comprising an area of 12.18 acres in plot No. 148 khatian 31/35, 93/31 (ka) Mouza Chalia JL No. 626 in Upazila Savar belonged to Dhaka Nawab Estabe and the land was given in settlement by the then Manager of the said Estate on 15-8-51 in favour of Abdus Samad, Abdur Rahman, Abdur Rashid who paid rent to the Nowab Estate Dhaka and they were recognized tenants and while Abdur Rahman and Abdur Rashid were possessing the land they sold 5.72 acres of land in plot No. 148 to Shahidur Rahman who mutated his name in the SA khatian in Misc. Case No. 5(b) of 73-74 for 5.72 acres. The name of Shahidur Rahman was also recorded in the RS Khatian. Thereafter Saidur Rahman sold 4.09 acres to the present petitioner by different registered kabalas and handed over the transferred land to the petitioner who thereafter mutated their names in the relevant SA Record of Right in Misc. Case No. 674(B)P-1/75-76 and paid rent and they developed the entire land and allotted the same to the members of the society. It is also the case of the present petitioner that during RS operation the plaintiff opposite parties filed Misc. Case No. 34.75 before the ADC (Rev.) Dhaka praying for mutation of their name in place of Sahidur Rahman which was ultimately rejected. The plaintiff opposite parties have no right title, and possession in the suit property and their kabalas were created with ulterior motive. 

 "All that pieces and parcel of 3.79 three acres and seventy nine decimals of land in plot No. 148 khatian No. 88 mouza No. 8673 and mouza No. 626 Salia under PS Savar Dist. Dhaka."

Rajdhani Unnayan Kartipakkha (RAJUK) ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Mir Nousher Ali ----- Opposite Party
fulldatas.full_judgment:
The petitioner obtained this Rule against the order dated June 15, 1991 passed by the Additional Assistant Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka allowing an application for amendment of the plaint of Title Suit No. 13 of 1991. 

 2. The application for amendment arose out of the following situation. The opposite party instituted the suit for permanent injunction on various allegations against the petitioner. His case was that the suit property along with other property belonged to Nowab Estate, Dhaka and subsequently was managed by Court of Wards. The opposite party after taking settlement of the suit land from the Chief Manager of Nowab Court of Wards was in possession on payment of Salami and rent. During his peaceful possession as owner, some of the employees of the petitioner tried to encroach upon the land on November 20, 1986. 

 3. The petitioner contested Title Suit No. 13 of 1991 by filing written statement denying the allegations made in the plaint. The case of the petitioner was that Major Khwaja Hasan Askhari, the Motwali of the Waqf Estate, on obtaining permission from the Administrator of Waqf transferred the land including the suit land to the United States of America by a registered deed of sale dated June 8, 1964 and the Embassy took possession of the land and was in peaceful possession. While the Embassy was in possession it entered into a talk at the Government level for exchange of its land with the land of Rajdhani Unnayan Kartipakha (RAJUK) situated at Baridhara. Pursuant to the talk delivery of possession of the land in suit including other lands was given to the erstwhile DIT. Thereafer the DIT fenced the area of the land with RCC pillars and barbed wires. The DIT, in its turn, also delivered possession of the land in Baridhara to the American Embassy followed by a deed of exchange which was executed and registered on May 21, 1984. The petitioner denied the right, title and interest and possession of the opposite party in the suit land.

fulldatas.lawyer:
Md. Abdul Zabbar, Advocate, instructed by Md. Nowab Ali, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Appellant 
Mrs. Rabia Bhuiyan, Senior Advocate, instructed by Md. Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record ----- For Respondent No. 1 
For Respondent Nos. 2-3 ----- Not Represented
fulldatas.parties:
A.B.M. Asgar ----- Appellant
Vs.
The Administrator and the Chairman of the Allotment Committee, Dhaka and others ----- Respondents
fulldatas.full_judgment:
2. The appellant instituted Writ Petition No. 471 of 1989 challenging the allotment of 47 shop rooms in the ground floor and 6 rooms in the 1st floor of Ahasanullah (Nawabbari) Super Market, Ahasan Manzi!, Dhaka by the respondents. According to the appellant there were 300 shop rooms in C.S. Plot Nos. 725-726 at the premises of Ahasan Manzil, Ahasanullah Road, Dhaka. The appellant and others shop owners had been carrying on their business in those shop rooms for a long time and earned their livelihood. The appellant took lease of a shop room from the Dhaka Nowab Court of Wards Estate in 1980. In 1985 the Government decided to acquire the historic Ahasan Manzil along with the lands of C.S. Plot No. 725-726 with a view to preserve and protect the said Ahasan Manzil as monument making necessary renovation thereof and to establish a museum thereon. After such acquisition the appellant along with 300 victim shop keepers became seriously affected. The affected shop keepers made a representation to various authorities including the President of the Republic and the then Chief Martial Law Administrator for saving them from total ruination with a suggestion that a Super Market should be constructed adjacent to the Ahasan Manzil monument where the shops were located on C.S. Plot No. 725- 726. The Government having found the proposal meaningful accepted the same and decided to construct a Super Market on the said plots adjacent to the Ahasan Manzil monument. 

 3. In the premises, the government by letter dated 18th January, 1986, directed the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka to take over and deliver the possession of the lands to the Dhaka City Corporation for construction of a Super Market thereon. In order to ensure that the shops in the said Super Market are made available to the affected shop keepers at the first instance by way of allotment on priority basis, the Government by letter dated 28th January, 1986, constituted a field survey committee. The said committee conducted a survey and prepared a list of affected shop keepers by physical verification and submitted its report to the Government on 15th February, 1986, and issued certificates to each of the affected shop keepers. Thereupon the Dhaka City Corporation took up construction work of the Super Market and with a view to meet the construction costs asked the affected shop keepers to pay salami of Tk. 25,000/- each in advance. The appellant and other shop keepers paid the salanii against receipts. Thereafter the City Corporation fixed the salami for a shop room at Tk. 1,50,000/- and asked the shop keepers to pay the balance amount by 5 equal installments of Tk. 25,000/-each. The appellant and other affected shop keepers duly paid the salami. 

 6. Their further case is that the affected shop keepers did not file appeal under section 155 of the Dhaka Municipal Corporation Ordinance, 1983, if they were at all aggrieved against the said allotment and therefore, the writ petition is not maintainable. Their further case is that all the allotees of the shop rooms in the ground floor having not been impleaded in the writ petitions, the appellant and other writ petitioners are not entitled to the relief, inasmuch as, if the said allotments were interfered with the said allotees would be adversely affected. 

 7. The High Court Division upon hearing the parties by the impugned judgment discharged the rule nisi observing that 317 shop keepers were affected by the acquisition of the lands and out of them 5 were land owners, 81 were tenants under the Dhaka Nowab Court of Wards Estate and remaining 231 were sub-tenants under the tenants of the said Estate. The learned Judges further  observed that there are 143 shop rooms in the basement, 140 in the ground floor, 141 in the 1st floor and 151 .in the 2nd floor, that the appellant or other affected shop keepers failed to prove that the City Corporation gave them any assurance to allot shop rooms in the ground floor of the Super Market and that the affected shop keepers including the appellant were given allotment of shop rooms either in the 1st floor or in the 2nd floor and they got possession of their respective shop rooms in February, 1988. 

 9. Mr. Md. Abdul Zabbar, the learned Counsel appearing for the appellant failed to show any material on record that the Dhaka City Corporation assured the affected shop keepers to allot shop rooms in the ground floor of the Super Market. The learned Counsel, however, contends that the City Corporation having allotted 48 shop rooms to outsiders including Barrister Rabeya Bhuiyan and the relations of the Administrator of the Dhaka City Corporation, who are not affected shop keepers, it is apparent that the alldtments have not been made fairly, and in an arbitrary manner and thus, those arbitrary allotments should have been declared to have been made or given to them without lawful authority. The learned counsel further contended that the appellant being an affected shop keeper and in view of the certificate issued of the field survey committee, he had acquired a vested right to get the allotment on priority basis in the ground floor but the learned Judges of the High Court Division failed to consider the said aspect of the matter and illegally dis-charged the rule nisi. 

 10. Annexue-D to the writ petition is a deed of undertaking given by Md. Abul Hossain, General Secretary, Nawab Bari Bastra Samity being counter signed by the President of the said Samity on 13th January, 1988 on behalf of the affected shop keepers. In pursuance of the said undertaking, the shops were allotted in presence of the Administrator Dhaka City Corporation on the basis of lottery on 10th January, 1988. The said lottery was held as per decision of the shop allotment committee providing that nobody would be entitled to raise any objection or institute any case against such allotments. Accordingly, the shops were allotted to the affected per-sons including the appellant by lottery. Annexure-B(3) showed that the appellant took possession of his shop room in the 2nd floor on 12th May, 1988 and after taking over possession, he instituted a writ petition in April 1989. There is also nothing on record to show that the City Corporation assured the appellant and other affected shop keepers to allot shop room in the ground floor of the Super Market. 

 12. The field survey committee issued certificate to the appellant and other affected persons for ascertaining the persons who were real affected persons by the acquisition of the lands with a view to allot shop rooms to them. This survey 'report does not accrue any vested right upon the affected shop keepers to have an allotment in the ground floor of the Super Market. Over and above, the appellant has not impleaded all the allottees who have got-ten shop rooms in the ground floor. These allottees have paid the premium and gotten possession of their respective rooms. The writ petition without impleading them as respondents is not legally maintainable, inasmuch as, the court can not give any declaration as prayed for in favour of the appellant without affording them an opportunity on being heard. Further, the appellant has not preferred any appeal as provided under section 155 of the Dhaka Municipal Corporation Ordinance, 1983. Section 154 of the Dhaka City Corporation Ordinance, 1983 provides that any person aggrieved by an order passed by the corroboration or any officer in pursuance of the said ordinance or rules or by laws may prefer an appeal to the pre-scribed authority within the period of limitation and any order passed in the appeal shall be final. If the appellant has got any grievance against the allotment, he could have preferred an appeal but without seeking redress to the proper authority in accordance with law moved the writ petition challenging the allotment. Without resorting to the alternative remedy available, the writ petition is not legally maintainable.

fulldatas.parties:
Moulvi Abullah Welfare Trust
Vs.
K.A. Gani, Advocate & Another
fulldatas.full_judgment:
The appellant Abdullah Welfare Trust got a decree against the Dhaka Nowab Court of Wards Estate on compromise in Title Suit No. 130 of 1957. The appellant started execution case for enforcement of the said decree and applied for delivery of possession of the decretal properties pending registration of the deeds by the judgment debtor but that was rejected by the Executing Court and the Executing Court appointed respondent No. 1 K.A. Gani as Receiver of the properties. The Receiver, it appears with court's permission started constructing a commercial building consisting of shop-rooms in the ground-floor in the land of Schedule A of the compromise decree but as he failed to render accounts of expenditures for the construction and of salami and rents received by way of disposal of the Shop-rooms the Executing Court by its order No. 265 dated 6-5-76 observed: 

 6. Abdullah Welfare Trust was created for the welfare and benefit of the Dhaka Nowab family. As it has been mentioned the said Welfare Trust obtained a compromise decree against the Dhaka Nowab Courts of Wards Estate in Title Suit No. 130 of 1957 and the decree was passed on 3-9-59. The decree contemplated registration of certain registered deed of transfer and transfer of possession of the decretal property to the appellant. The appellant applied for delivery of possession but since the registration of the deeds was not complied the Executing Court by its order dated 20-7-73 appointed respondent as a Receiver under section 41(d) read with rule 1 of Order 40 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It appears that the Receiver with Court's permission started constructing commercial building consisting of shop-room in the land of Schedule A of the decree. He disposed of some shops by receiving salami and rent but he did not render any account of expenditure either for construction or of the receipt of money by way of salami and rent whereupon the Executing Court expressed its dissatisfaction by order dated 6-5-76. It has already been mentioned Contractor N. Ahmed pressed for his dues from the respondent and ultimately this matter came before the High Court Division in C.R. No. 840 of 1976 when the High Court Division in its judgment dated 3-8-76 directed the Executing Court to effect delivery of possession to the appellant on their furnishing bank guarantee to Tk. 3,50,000/-. This order was frustrated because in the meantime a move was made by the Receiver for appointment of a joint Receiver in the person of Khawaja Mohiuddin who however, could not function as he died immediately thereafter. Hence the sole Receiver Khawja Abdul Gani continued to function as a Receiver. In 1979 the Board of Trustee were constituted after duly held election and in the meantime document, in question were also registered. Hence the appellant again prayed for delivery of possession in pursuance of the order of the High Court Division passed in C.R. 840 of 1976 and prayed for direction upon the Receiver to submit upto date statement of account on income and expenditure and further prayed for stopping payment to the Receiver till the accounts were finally settled. The Receiver resisted this petition for delivery of possession and he submitted his accounts for the period 1974 to 1980 on 29-9-80. The Receiver gave a summary of his account vide Annexure A. These accounts were, however, challenged by the appellants who had it audited by an accountant which is also annexed as annexure B to B(6). The Executing Court, however, it seems, passed order No. 419 dated 26-11-80 : 

 15. Next as has been mentioned Rule 3 of the Order 40 enjoins upon the Court to hold the Receiver to correct strictness in rendering their accounts and thorough investigation of the accounts supported by voucher is proper. Mere submission of the accounts is not enough. It must be seen whether he has spent the money as per direction of the court. In Coomer Sattya Sankar Ghosal V. Rance Golapmonce Debia 5 C.W. N. 223 it was held that when a Receiver had submitted his account it is the duty of the court to see, not merely whether, all the collections have been duly entered in the accounts and the expenses supported by vouchers but also whether all the disbursements and payments are properly made in respect of the estate. In Hooper Versus Winston the contention of the Receiver that he had some discretionary power was negatived and it was held- 

 18. What does a Court do when passes account of Receiver ? It means that the Court calls upon the Receiver first to produce and file his account which are checked with proper vouchers and other proofs before the Accounting Officer and thereafter they are pressed before the Court which passes them. In passing such account the court must be taken to approve and sanction both the credit and the debit entries made in that account. When the court gives authority to the Receiver to advance money for the benefit of the estate of which he is the Receiver and sanction such advance he is entitled to an indemnity out of the assets for that advance. In Boehm V. Goodall (1911) ICh. 155 it was observed: 

 20. In view of the aforesaid we are of the opinion that the case must be remitted to the Executing Court in order that the accounts of the Receiver for the entire period of his management may be taken: A firm of Chartered Accountants must be appointed for this purpose and the said Firm will be authorised not only to verify whether the expenditure is supported by proper vouchers but also to determine whether sums received by the Receiver have been properly credited to the Estate and spent for the legitimate purpose. The objection to the account when submitted before the Court should be formulated with precision and for this purpose every facility will be afforded to the parties and their legal advisers to examine accounts, vouchers and all connected papers so as to enable them to draw up their objection and the Executing Court upon consideration of this objection will draw a final order for adjusting the right and liability of the parties and the Receiver. It is to be clearly understood that in the end, if it transpires that the claims of the creditors exhausted the amount in respect of which the Receiver is entitled to be reimbursed the liability must fail upon the Receiver himself. In view of the above, we direct as under: 

 (3) The Account of the Trust during the entire tenure of the Receiver will be audited by a firm of Chartered Accountants, namely M/s Rahman Huq & Co., 82 Motijheel C.A,. Dhaka 2.
